text:
@gibber1944  As a shareholder do you understand the fine details of manufacturing costs, what it means to use TSMC vs. Samsung, having a huge monolithic die vs. smaller tiles/chiplets? Do you understand that manufacturing costs have gone up by about 20% in general since the end of 2020?

Do you know Biden is reinstating the 25% tariff that was in place for all of 2021 for GPUs?

Do you know the 4090 sells out immediately as soon as there is new stock and that's a GPU making higher profit margin?

Do you know Nvidia cut the number of wafers from TSMC for the next year?  In other words they projected a slow down and they don't want to overproduce?


In other words I think Nvidia is doing what they can do with what it is they're making and considering there is now a slowdown in sales of PC equipment across the board, they're probably handling it about the best they can regardless of 4080s not selling out immediately.  It's not like AMD GPU are going to fly off shelves when it's rare they have more than 10% of graphics card sales.  Sure, their first wave of GPUs will probably move pretty well, and it's going to happen regardless of the price of the 4080 because a lot of people want to buy AMD GPUs.  But reality will set in for AMD too and 2023 isn't going to be a good year for GPU sales with the US imposing a 25% tariff once again.  I don't know where the Founders GPUs come out of but if they come out of Taiwan Nvidia will do well selling their own GPU, but a few of their AIBs that manufacture in China are going to suffer.  If Nvidia GPUs come out of China also, then Nvidia Founders GPUs won't sell all that great either because they'll cost MORE, not less.


So if you're going to invest in a tech company, it's good to understand details and not simply make a statement about cost like what reviewers do, who don't analyze the markets.

text:
Upscaling on cards that are still very high-end (4080, 7900XTX) is kinda silly, both of these cards generate so much performance, it just doesnt make sense, so while FSR is "fine" and DLSS is "better" you still lose visual quality and frame consistency with both, so on cards where you dont really need extra performance like these, it really does not make sense to use either.

Also frame consistency is actually a unique place where FSR is actually a fair bit better than DLSS, FSR just tends to have a smoother and more consistent delivery of each frame.

And Frame Gen is just a stupid gimmick, you gain so much input lag it makes it almost unusable, so only really makes sense on ultra-low end cards where you aare just trying to sqeeze out all the performance you can get.

I don't feel like AMD has done a good job pushing Nvidia at all.

Just want to Add, and people have to be aware, and paging to those new AMD Radeon 7000 Buyers. Please if your game supports Ray Tracing, TURN IT OFF. So I believe this is where majority of the Reviewer fall short, because they compare it RT off on different slides then On on a different slides, so it doesn't look good for Radeon. BUT if you compare the games on "Radeon FSR+RT off+(probably SAM if available in your system)" vs. "NVidia's DLSS+RT on" ON THE SAME SLIDES it changes greatly, and people will be aware as well on what settings to use for their Radeon card to get to those high FPS number.

text:
The Hog Rider card is unlocked from the Spell Valley (Arena 5). He is a quick building-targeting, melee troop with moderately high hitpoints and damage. He appears just like his Clash of Clans counterpart; a man with brown eyebrows, a beard, a mohawk, and a golden body piercing in his left ear who is riding a hog. A Hog Rider card costs 4 Elixir to deploy.

Strategy

His fast move speed can boost forward mini tanks like an Ice Golem in a push. At the same time, he can also function as a tank for lower hitpoint troops such as Goblins as he still has a fair amount of health. Most cheap swarms complement the Hog Rider well, as they are nearly as fast as him and usually force more than one card out of the opponent's hand.

The Hog Rider struggles with swarms, as they can damage him down and defeat him quickly while obstructing his path. Barbarians in particular can fully counter him without very strict timing on the defender's part, though be wary of spells.

A Hunter can kill the Hog Rider in 2 hits if placed right on top of it. However, if you place something in front of the Hog Rider, the Hunter's splash will damage the Hog Rider and hit the card in front of it more.

A good placement and timing with Guards and The Log will fully counter the Hog Rider, canceling all Hog hits.

The Hog Rider in conjunction with the Freeze can surprise the opponent and allow the Hog Rider to deal much more damage than anticipated, especially if the opponent's go-to counter is a swarm, or swarms are their only effective counter to him. text:
Really nice video again as always, thank you Steve and team! 
I wanted to pose a question, but let me first give some context. When making a new build for a given budget, I often run into the problem that I have to open multiple review pages or search through reviews to find each of the parts I am considering with some performance/power/etc in the same graph/testing methodology. For example, say that for the current budget and availability I am looking at a 3070 Ti, 2080 Super and 6700XT, this comes up especially when looking at second hand market as well. 
I know that  a review publisher such as yourself most likely has all the data I am looking for, but does not put it into any single graph because its such an unusual comparison and there is only so much screen space. However, it would be very useful if said data would be published on your website at least in some part, to make it easier for consumers to do this kind of comparison and maybe make it easier to evaluate if a second hand last-gen offer is a good deal versus current-gen new options. Since you are an advocate of reducing e-waste, I am really hoping that this fits your ideals in making second hand purchasing more straightforward. 
Thank you very much for taking the time to read this.

THERMAL TEST please Steve: (pretty please consider) Every time I see this cooler layout, I feel that it would work better if the rear edge (mobo side) was just sealed off. 
1/2 of the exhausted air is hitting the motherboard and with nowhere else to go is being fed straight back into the cooler (compounding) every time.

text:
Detailed review, but two aspects bothered me: 

8K gaming is not an empty thing to boast about since already in 2023 there will be 8K monitors and TVs, while you have a connector that can enable the resolution at high refresh rate, though I very much hope even one of those TVs will utilize DisplayPort, which is very much possible. Running lighter games like Rocket League or perhaps indie games (let alone desktop enviroment) is really a compelling thing to do on such a high resolution and if the card can reach even acceptable 4K performance, then FSR will do the rest on an 8K screen, since such high resolutions are where these scaling techniques excel and are actually meant for.

Other thing is the meaningless comparison between past high end products like RX Vega 64 and RX 5700 XT to the RX 7900 XTX. If one is not a pure fanboy, you buy your GPU typically based on how much you can and are willing to spend and how much performance you desire, opposed to simply picking the absolute best that one brand offers. RX 5700 XT buyers (like me) bought the card because it cost just over 400 €, while Nvidia absolutely dominated the enthusiast segment back then. Such customers are far from a potential buyer of a 1000 € GPU, no matter how high inflation might be. The only Radeon card that RX 7900 XTX can and should properly be compared to is naturally the RX 6900/6950 XT.

Thanks for the data. Cheers!

For Gamers that stick with Nvidia: 
Stop sweating over Ray Tracing. 
If you want to play your games at 4K (well, 3.8K) ultra/maxxed presets at 120fps with ray tracing on, then come back maybe two or 3 cards from now, and maybe ray tracing won't be so much of a gimmick by then. Try the RTX 6090 LOL

I kept my 1080ti while everyone else seemed to be sprinting out to grab up 2xxx-series cards. It was so funny. I absolutely skipped the 2080ti.
I of course bought two RTX Titans (since i always collected them), and even with the RTX Titans, ray tracing was a gimmick. 

If you can't help yourself with ray tracing, and just HAVE TO have it, then don't buy anything less than the top end card. 
My advice though, is stop sweating over it right now. Don't get caught up in the ray tracing churn machine. The incremental improvements aren't worth the money at all.

text:
Yeah for Christ's sake I don't carte about freaking upscaling, that smudgy blurry slurred mess isn't cutting it and it's really nuts to me seeing this top of the line hardware literally not even hitting 60fps sometimes WITH the fuckin upscaler on. Like just look at the 2080ti, Jesus Christ. I'd have felt so ripped off if I bought 20 series for RT. It's basically unplayable without DLSS 2.0 and 30 series or better, even for 1080p apparently. And if I'm buying a thousand dollar card in 2023 or 2024 you bet your ass I expect--not want, expect--it to be able to play new games at 4k. Like. I am not buying a brand new thousand dollar GPU to play fucking 1080p my dude, I am not, I don't care how pretty RT allegedly looks on some title, I've never seen it look nice enough to justify those prices and that awful performance.

What's the funniest thing about it all is that fully pathtraced scenes do justify that to me, it's just that not even a 4090 can do the Overdrive pathtracing yet. So what we're stuck with is 4k gaming still being basically out of reach of the average consumer. Anyone who's got the money to pay for that shit is probably too busy litigating and stitching shut chest cavities to have the time to bother with what would be a multithousand dollar setup, that even if I were making 100k a year spending 4-5k on a system isn't quite worth it if you're not even home to play it because you're too busy working. This is sort of the conundrum about high end gaming in general though, that the people who have the time and money are probably at the sweetspot right before they had kids and/or a real career, just before that, but right after having some kind of real job that still doesn't require more than fulltime employment. Which basically makes anything that's not a 7700XT or 4070 pretty niche when it comes to 4k, so trying to call it "8k ready" is such a fucking farce dude. I mean yeah--if you're playing F.E.A.R. 2 on a $5,000 USD system sure. If it's even Witcher 3, good luck with that. Which is all the more bullshittery when you consider that nVidia basically pushed CDPR to try and come up with some more excuses to get new hardware by getting the game that ran on a GTX 770 2gb at 1080p to be fucking unplayable at 1440p with a 3080, gj. Sorry I'm just so jaded at this point. Like, I'm at the point I'd basically just like to dick around playing Blood and Wine DLC on a 4k panel, that cost me less than $300, and can be powered with a $500 GPU. I really don't give a shit about trying to get raytracing to work on Phantom Liberty at this time, it's clear to me that even a 4080 or 7900XTX is going to run like ass and I'd much rather just turn off all the upscaling at that point. 

To be fair, I'll give credit where it's due, DLSS 3 isn't quite so godawful as the ripoff that was Turing, and FSR is just yeesh. FSR 1.0 is pretty bad on Cyberpunk. I mean it's not horrible, it still looks ok enough but the problem is shit like FSR and DLSS is mainly useful if you have a GTX 1650 max-Q or 1060 on a laptop that legitimately can't play it and your literal only choice is to either upscale and have blurriness, or turn all things down to low and 720p so it looks like complete shit anyway, or just not get to play it because you're running 15fps at high settings. That's the one damn time I see DLSS as being useful and of course DLSS is not available on that hardware anyway, so the only reason to be excited about upscaling is having a 3050 laptop and playing Phantom Liberty, OR using AMD tech on nVidia hardware. So yes DLSS does look marginally better, but not by enough to care for the hardware that can use it, when DLSS still makes things look worse and I'd rather just turn off all the gimmicks and run high resolution native if I'm not being forced to use FSR on a GTX 970m on a decade old laptop. Like if DLSS works with a GTX 980m that'd actually be cool, because it doesn't suck so hard that I'd rather turn down settings to low and my resolution to 900p. However I'd still rather run medium to high Witcher 3 settings and get 42fps on an old laptop, or play Cyberpunk 2077 at 1440p at 42fps using a 5700XT or 1080ti, than having to either use FSR or drop resolutions and settings. So it's stupid because I'm already the sort of person who's willing to sacrifice frames just to get the prettier graphics, and I personally would rather not upscale. Which defeats the whole point. Why tf would I spend thousands of dollars on hardware only to run bad fps AND have weird shimmering, artifacting, and muddy shit going on when it rains? Which is the same exact deal for ultra high resolution, like do I need to see Geralt's pores blur and shimmer in 8k?

author: @land.1368

text:
@land.1368  It's not really luck of the draw, it mostly depends on the input filtering of the card. Manufacturers can change the resonance frequency by adding capacitors, but it increases the cost (f = 1/2π√ (LC)). Different power supplies can also change the coil whine because of different ripple characteristics on the 12V rail. Buildzoid has some nice reviews of the power delivery of certain cards.
Basically it doesn't depend on the individual card, and more on how the AIB decides to design it.

text: I wonder how long it'll be until real-time raytracing is a refined, mature technology. First we need to catch up to pure rasterized performance, so that's probably 2-3 product generations out, maybe 5 years or so. Then we need to increase ray density by probably at least 4-16x to have a hope of eliminating disocclusion/accumulation noise - probably another 3-5 product generations, assuming continued exponential gains from a combination of both silicon and software/driver improvements. At some point we'd ideally switch over to pure raytracing instead of the current hybrid renderers with raytraced lighting, reflections, and effects overlaid on top of rasterized geometry, and this'll require even more performance gains to make practical. We're looking at 20-30 years. At least Steve's got job security?

author: @HeavyMetalGamingHD

text:
@HeavyMetalGamingHD  Right, but at the same time, the reference models have only two 8-pin power connectors with most custom models having three 8-pin power connectors.   This means the custom models can supply more power to the GPU for higher clock speeds.    The reference models were set up specifically to counter the huge size of the NVIDIA cards, but this came with trade-offs.   Smaller cooler due to smaller video card size being a goal, to keep the cards from getting too hot, they had to limit how fast the GPU itself could run, so limit power delivery.

Go to the Sapphire 7900XTX Vapor-X as an example of a GOOD 7900XTX that isn't getting artificially limited by trying to make a smaller card.

text:
Gonna be a bit nostalgic here.
The state of GPU prices compelled me to check back on two of my favourite launches of the past: the HD4870 and the 7970.  I really liked the "Let's start with the price point most people buy at and just ace it" approach of the 4870 small die launch.  I ran the launch MSRP of $300 through the Bank of Canada Inflation Calculator and that puts it at just over $400 in 2022 dollars.  The closest launch MSRP and die size equivalent earlier this year would be the 6650XT.  I know an apples to apples comparison in performance is hard when featuresets change so much and one of those apples is 14 years old, but the 4870 sat much higher in charts back then than the 6650XT did last year.
The higher end, bigger die release of the HD7970 at $550MSRP in 2012 (Just under $700 in 2022 dollars) was also good value for the money.  The 7950 at $450 was arguably even better.  Both of them traded blows with the more expensive 590 and 580s.  Even accepting that the 7900XTX is at a tier or two higher than the 7970 in its day, I think we'd be lucky to see that kind of value at the predicted prices I'm seeing for the 7800XT and 7700XT.

I know the fact that prices have drastically outpaced CPI (and incomes) is old news, but I thought it'd be helpful to make that value comparison.  Offering better value than the 4080 and 4090 is a good start but that's far short of where we could be.

author: @pedromvuus

text:
@someguy3186  I have a reply to Flaming Scar's post that I didn't post.  You're gonna get all of it, and I'm so sorry.

I don't know what their professional field is, and mine is only peripheral to those you mentioned, but we do have some layperson factchecking tools for things like commodity prices.  I suggest you look at the historical changes in copper and aluminum.  They rose dramatically in 2006 and, notwithstanding recessions and the 2016 price FlamingScar may or may not have cherry-picked, they have been in comparable ranges to 2008 when the 4870 launched, so I don't think they contribute significantly to the CPI-adjusted price change.  I couldn't find any good long-term data for silicon wafers, unfortunately.  I also suggest you (and @FlamingScar) look into the geophysical scarcity (more geology and economics than geopolitics, though the latter can affect market availability) of copper and aluminum. I care about the depletion of scarce elements too, but aluminum is the third most abundant metal on earth, there is lots of copper, and silicon is in every rock out there; sand is silicon (close enough).  We are not running out of those elements.

I'll bring up the 6650 XT again.  In terms of materials, including die size and PCB, it is comparable to the 4870.  The main material difference is the cooler.  More aluminum, less copper (compared to my Sapphire 4850), whatever fluid is in the heatpipes, and the manufacturing complexity.  The 256mm2 4870 was able to do incredibly the 521mm2 NVIDIA 580 in many at 150W.  The 4850 wasn't far behind and it managed with a single slot cooler.  My Sapphire 4850 didn't even cover the whole PCB and did just fine.

So what am I getting at?  I'm not convinced metal commodity prices account for the price difference.  

That said, I acknowledge that the RV770 vs the GT200 was a moment where AMD simply had an efficiency advantage over NVIDIA on every metric, and that we can't have that at every generation.  

What we are seeing is that both companies are selling us much more silicon mm2 AND power draw, impacting the material cost of the coolers - to perform well at todays games.  Maybe the missing variable here is how the demands of the applications are exceeding BOTH manufacturers' price:performance ratios.

text:
MSRP is one thing, beeing able to buy the GPU for the advertised price is another!

Back in the day it used to be that you could simply order the card for the MSRP after launch and if you waited a few months you yould get it for a discount or a better OC/custom card for the MSRP of the reference model. These days you have to be quick or hope for "drops"/"special offers" to get one of the few cards they actually sell at MSRP,  otherwise you will have to pay the market adjusted (=scalper) price.

It may be different in your market, but in mine (Germany), it currently looks like this: AMDs MSRP for the 7900 XT is 1050€ and for the XTX it's 1150€. The XTX was sold out immediatly and by the time I got home from work, the prices for the very few available cards already adjusted to 4080-levles (about 1350-1450€). The XT is still available in multiple online shops, but they now sell at or above the MSRP of the XTX, so no, thank you.

If you ask me, that's by design: AMD launches a good product and advertise it for a very good price compared to the competition - everybody is stoked and cheers for AMD, hurray!  But then only make 1 for every 5 or 10 they know they could sell and watch as the prices rise to the level they actually wanted the product to sell for and everybody blames "the scalpers" for it, but not the real culprit, AMD.

Keep in mind: due to high energy prices, large scale mining never really occured here, so there aren't scores of miner-GPUs flooding the used market, putting pressure on Nvidia/AMD to lower prices to a more reasonable level.

text: The voltage drop on the PCIE power connector input is not something the card can affect without reducing power. It is simply result of PSU cable resistance and the voltage on the side of the PSU. Every cable acts as a resistor and has some amount of voltage drop, this drop depends only on the resistance of the cable and the current flowing through it. So the only way to reduce the voltage drop without changing the PSU or the PSU cable is by reducing the amount of power the GPU is pulling, thus reducing the current. That is not something that would be desirable unless the voltage drops really low (that might hint and improperly connected cables for example) and should not be an issue unless the PSU cable is really bad, in that case we might get melting cables 😀

author: @thatrandomguycommenting1261

text:
It all comes down to total power consumption, and the quality of the inductors/VRMs used.

A 6700XT draws just over 200W, whereas 6900XTs can approach 350W.

The extra power means there's exponentially more physical resonance noise coming from the VRMs that supply the power. Especially if they're not sufficiently damped inside the inductor packages (the grey rectangular boxes near the GPU die), or if they're not high quality coils inside these inductor packages to begin with.

text: AMD has actually managed to release cards that somehow make the 4080 look like a better value, no wonder there was complete radio silence from them after the presentation and during the presentation they didn't seem particularly excited to begin with and now we know why. Higher power draw, check. Worse transient power spikes, check. More often than not worse performance in rasterization versus the card it's supposed to go up against, check. Worse thermals, check. Significantly worse ray tracing performance, check. God awful coil whine, check. From a fully encompassing viewpoint outside of just gaming, a worse feature set and less applicable use cases, check. This is most certainly not and I quote from the countless people shouting from the rooftops on Reddit "A 4080 / 4090 killer that's within 10% - 15% of the performance of the 4090" I was really looking forward to buying a Radeon GPU this generation, but after what I've seen I would rather get a 4080 / 4090 and wouldn't touch the 7900 XTX with a 10 foot pole for $1000. In the grand scheme of things, it's actually a much worse value with its only redeeming factor being the increase in VRAM. I'm fully convinced now that something went terribly wrong with the architecture during the manufacturing of these cards hence why they've got a 7900 XTX that should realistically be listed as an 80 class card at absolute best, then you've got AIB cards being able to get hardly any extra performance out of having an additional 8-pin connector pushing power to the board (at least not enough performance to make any meaningful difference for the increase in cost). This is truly heartbreaking, and has made it very apparent that AMD won't be able to push anything out this generation that will come close to the 4090 as an in-generation refresh, clocking in at a roughly 40% performance increase with a in-generation refresh is unheard of.

I don’t know about new FSR so this might be a negligible or nonexistent problem but FSR in the past had noticeably lower quality video output at any given setting when compared to DLSS. If that’s still the case, AMD is in an even worse place in these comparisons than is shown

text:
Just an FYI, while the 7950XTX would probably still make a decent profit at $700
The 12GB 4080 now 4070TI is an even worse cash grab.
"Moore's law is dead"-Jensen Wang
Ok, Moore's law is dead, thats why the technical successor to the 3090 is 6% more expensive, both cards are roughly 600mm² with a 384 bit bus and 24GB of RAM
While i didnt like the $1500 price point, a mere 6% price increase is more than reasonable considering most parts being used are more expensive.......

HOWEVER
When you price the technical successor to the 12GB RTX 3060, at $900 and name it a 4080, you're not just pissing on the customer's head and telling them it is raining, you're serving them urine slushees telling them it is a limited edition pickled flavor

Both the 12GB 3060, and the 12GB 4080, now 70TI are less than 300mm² have a very narrow 192 bit bus.
This is a smaller memory bus and die than many previous 60 cards, and this is the only card in Nvidia's history to carry a name higher than XX60 to only come with a 192 bit bus.
If the 4090 is only $1600, then this card should be $355, instead it is priced at $900

Nvidia does this every time they have a monopoly on performance. Just look at the GTX 1080 and Vega 64. The GTX 1080 was technically a 60 classs die, with a 70/80 class memory bus (like the 2060 or the 3060TI), but because AMD could only compete with Nvidia's mid-range XX60 die, Nvidia was free to re-name, and re-price the 1060, to the 1080, and the 1070/1080 were free to be re-named to the 1080TI and Titan XP

I can guarantee that if the Vega 64 competed with the Titan XP, that the Titan XP name would never have existed(or used the full 100 die) and the card we bought as the Titan XP would at best have been called the 1080, because Nvidia, cannot have their highest end consumer brand beaten by a competitor, and they sure as heck can never allow the Titan to be bested.

Honestly, i bought an A770 for tinkering, and now i think i'm just going to use it out of principle None of these companies deserve my money. Yes i realize that the market determines the price, but mining has dried up, only the 4090 can demand this kind of price in a normal market, but we're not in a normal market, people have less money to spend on items like this, really if these cards were priced appropriately, the 16GB 4080 would be $649, the 4070TI would be $300

text:
What does "It's not 100% test" even mean?  I think you left out the word "Accurate".  What good is being 100% accurate, when you are accounting for all the wrong things?  And since when is 100% even necessary when there's a range of tolerances, or where the difference between more or less of something makes no measurable difference?

You sound like an audiophile getting their panties in a knot over frequency ranges outside of human hearing, or some guitar player who thinks the type and amount of paint on their electric guitar makes any measurable difference, let alone an audible one!

Who said they don't have the assembly specs (Order and torque) if they even matter anywhere near to the same degree as on cylinder heads?  They don't!

In the case of an engine it's about maintaining good seals, and preventing premature wear by eliminating physical distortion of the cylinder heads, not better heat dissipation.   Here you are not trying to counter pressure with pressure, have no relevant moving parts and whatever forces they bring to worry about, nor need to worry about heat distorting the plate at these temps and it's relative size, and finally:  Once the screws bottom out, there's already enough pressure (by design), and any extra torque is only to keep the screws from coming loose.

That pattern may show distortion or inaccurate dimensions of the plate or components themselves, to where adjusting the torque of a few screws, including taking some pressure off of one or more may be beneficial.

text: My 6900 XT whines like crazy too, I always use Vsync for most games so the GPU would not produce waste frames, but in heavy games under load coil whining is constant. Can I quite it down with new PSU or something?
author: @DeathCoreGuitar

text:
Use Freesync rather than Vsync since you are losing performance otherwise if you dip under the monitor's maximum refresh rate.

If you don't have Freesync, then turn off Vsync and just use a framerate limiter instead.

As for the coil whine, wear some closed-back headphones or earphones. Close the panels on your PC case, put the PC on the floor, or on the other side of your desk. Splitting the power across different PCIE cables to the GPU can also help (use a separate PCIE power cable for each 8-pin on the GPU).

You can try to swap out the PSU for another, which might help, or could make it worse. It's not guarenteed to fix or reduce the problem, even if it's a high-end PSU. It all depends on how the PSU pairs with the quality of the inductors/VRMs on the GPU.
author: @Fed-Up-YouTuber

text: ​ @Fed-Up-YouTuber  Thank you for your time but almost everything you wrote is not helpful or just not true
author: @DeathCoreGuitar

text:
@DeathCoreGuitar  I appreciate your response as well, but let me know what's not true. Everything I said is either verified through my experience, or through research that's been stated by an electrician in laymen terms.

Everything down to the grid quality and load of your wall outlet can influence coil whine, and that's not even counting the power delivery characteristics of the PSU itself. This is why splitting the load across multiple PCIE power rails can sometimes help reduce coil whine.

Not an insignificant amount of people have bought new PSUs to try to minimize GPU coil whine with mixed results, sometimes it's better, sometimes it's the same, or sometimes it's worse, even with Gold or Platinum rated PSUs.

Without changing anything hardware-wise, the best you can do is set a framerate limiter and undervolt/underclock your GPU (or set a lower power target).

text:
@mjkittredge  8k in general is dumb. In fact having anything more than 1440p on a 27 inch display or 4k on a 32 inch display is a waste of pixels considering that you have to sit uncomfortably close to the monitor to actually be able to notice the finer detail beyond placebo affect (assuming 20/20 vision) for resolutions any higher. Let's say for example your head is about 2 feet 1 inch from your 4k display, at this distance a 32 inch display is optimal to fully appreciate the 4k detail without noticing individual pixels and breaking the illusion of a continuous image. Do you know how much larger an 8k display would need to be for the detail to be fully appreciated at that viewing distance? You would need to be sitting around 2 feet one inch away from a 65 inch monitor to appreciate the detail of 8k. The only practical use of 8k is for video editing to a 4k final product, or for VR where you are extremely close to the display and it takes up your whole field of view. But for general gaming and content consumption, unless you want to give your neck muscles a really good workout and your panel has extreme viewing angles. A 16:9 8k display is a waste of money. 
Obviously curved displays are exempt. Going wider than 4k on a curved ultra wide works just fine, although you still have the problem of having to physically turn your head to fully appreciate the detail of the image towards the edges of the monitors.

text:
latest game engines are so optimized by default that a 1070 can run almost anything with decent graphics and frames.

I have a 1070TI and run everything on Highest with locked 50 frames per second and 100 hrz free-sync monitor.
(your eye will not see the difference between 60 frames and 50 frames, so until you do don't fall for marketing gimmicks)

The only reason to bump it to 120 hrz and 60 frames is if you are playing a competitive game on a network, and even then, you would be hard pressed to notice a difference.
Your connection will always be the bottleneck before anything else.

As long as you keep your frame rate locked you guarantee maximum performance, minimum energy consumption and increased card life.
Keep the monitor frequency at double your locked frame rate so you have a stable 2 hrz per frame, this also improves performance and increased monitor life.
Disable v-sync in-game because your free-sync monitor is doing the job already = max performance.
If you are playing at a desk, you do not need 4k or a big monitor because it will hurt your neck and eyes, get a 27" or a 32".
RT is a gimmick, what you get will never pay for the loss in performance. When it gets down to: RT ON= lose less than 10 frames start to consider it viable, else let them work on it for a few more years. + rasterization has improved a lot too, that it is hard to tell which one is which.

text:
@chrente  lol from 60hrz to 120hrz the difference is the same as 60hrz to 240hrz.
Increasing hrz, all it does it reduces tearing on fast moving actions.  Once you have 2 hrz per frame and the frame rate is stable and locked, you won't see a difference since there is no tearing between frames on fast scenes. That is all business.
Hrz = how many times the pixels on the screen refresh themselves, thus they need to match the frame rate to give best performance. Thus 1.5 refresh per frame is bad. That is why you should never have a 144 hrz while running a 100 FPS locked, because it would be a 1.44 hrz per frame. Thus a lot of correction needs to happen which creates tearing and loss of performance.
(some frames will get 1 refresh(hrz) and some will get 2)
 
Always have a multiple of the frame rate.
60 FPS can have 120hrz or 180hrz or 240hrz or 300 hrz
120hrz will always be better than 330 hrz for 60 FPS.
60hrz monitor is only 1 hrz per frame which is bad since any movement of FPS will create tearing and lag because it would have less than 1 refresh for a frame.
Once you go 120hrz that will go away.
If you are running 50FPS then 100 hrz is just the same.

BTW
I am a hard core gamer and played many FPS games like Unreal Tournament 2004.
I know what competitive gaming is and was quite good at it too.

text:
@GamersNexus  And another thing, 8K performance should get a lot better with new software support, Variable Rate Shading is particularly well suited to ultra high resolutions, if the player is really only concerned with having maximal sharpness around the crosshairs then VRS will let you do that with minimal performance cost, and in general the benefits of VRS over running full native resolution only becomes more dramatic as resolution increases.
Of course VRS implementations are so rare that it makes no difference to the market today, but someday the performance cost of 8K is going to look a lot more reasonable than it does right now.
author: @budthecyborg4575

text: @GamersNexus  Also also, try running 8K benchmarks on games from six/seven years ago, everyone has a library full of games that will run amazingly well at 8K on this card.
author: @budthecyborg4575

text: @GamersNexus  Also also also, games like Elden Ring can scale by resolution but not framerate, so there are scenarios where increasing resolution is your only option for making use of a more powerful GPU.
author: @budthecyborg4575

text:
@GamersNexus  After buying the 7900XTX I was testing RE4 Remake at 200% render target (8K) on my LG OLED and it gets around 45fps, not great but if I had an 8K display I would have been able to turn on FSR Quality and get a sharp 8K output at around 100fps.
8K gaming is not a gimmick, it's actually the best way to leverage all the upscaling tech that we have.
